newsitem.title: USA: Once Hollywood powerbroker, Ovitz now unemployed.
newsitem.headline: Once Hollywood powerbroker, Ovitz now unemployed.

text.p: He rose from lowly studio tour guide to become one of Hollywood's most powerful executives. But Michael Ovitz will soon be out of a job.

Ovitz said Thursday he will resign, effective Jan. 31, from his post as president of the Walt Disney Co., the second highest office in the world's second largest entertainment company, behind Time Warner Inc.

In a statement, Disney said the decision was by "mutual agreement," but Ovitz's departure came after much speculation in the industry and media that he and Disney Chairman Michael Eisner were at odds over how best to run the company.

Ovitz joined Disney in August 1995 amid great fanfare over his ability to strengthen its ties with the top talent in the industry, and he was assigned the job of overseeing Disney's three operating units -- filmed entertainment, theme parks and consumer products.

At the time, he and Eisner were described as longtime friends who would run Disney as partners. But industry sources said both men have had trouble adjusting to their new relationship because both are accustomed to being in charge.

"I doubt if he feels like a true partner," said one industry insider about Ovitz. "Eisner is obviously a strong-willed guy and clearly wants to leave his stamp on the company. It will probably take many, many years for him to view someone as an equal partner."

Indeed in its announcement, Disney said it will leave the president's position open as it had before Ovitz joined the company. Prior to Ovitz, the president's post had been filled by long-time Disney executive Frank Wells, who died in a helicopter crash in 1994.
Ovitz has fallen far from his heyday at the helm of the powerful Creative Artists Agency, which helped fashion the careers of stars like Tom Hanks, Tom Cruise and Barbra Streisand.

A husband and father of two, Ovitz grew up in a middle-class household in suburban San Fernando Valley outside Los Angeles. He studied pre-med at the University of California, Los Angeles, but first glimpsed behind-the-scenes Hollywood as as a tour guide at Universal Studios.
The deal-making agency business lured Ovitz into its ranks with a job in the William Morris Agency mailroom, where movie business kingpins like Barry Diller and David Geffen started.
Ovitz quickly rose from mailroom employee to television agent, but in 1975 left the William Morris Agency to co-found Creative Artists.

As head of the agency, Ovitz helped usher in the age of programme "packaging" in which an agent puts together writer, producer, director and star in one package, then sells the show or movie to a television network or film studio.
His deal-making ability earned him the reputation as the most powerful man in Hollywood.

Ovitz's ambition, however, ran higher than merely brokering deals for stars. Increasingly, in the merger mania of the 1980s, Ovitz began manoeuvring his agency into position as a highly paid broker of business deals.
In 1989, he helped electronics giant Sony Corp. acquire Columbia Pictures from Coca-Cola Co. in a $3.4 billion deal.

One year later, he advised Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. Ltd. on its $6.6 billion purchase of MCA/Universal, now called Universal Studios Inc. Then in 1995, he turned around and assisted in Matsushita's sale of the studio to Seagram Co. Ltd. for $5.7 billion.

The Seagram deal, though, led to one of the lowest points in Ovitz's career. Ovitz went through weeks of negotiations with Seagram Chief Executive Officer Edgar Bronfman to run the movie studio, theme park and music operations. But talks broke down over issues of money and company control.
